summary: Describes privacy extensions for IPv6 stateless address autoconfiguration. Rather than deriving the interface identifier from a hardware identifier, a node can generate temporary changing ones to make tracking harder. It is a draft standard, replaced by RFC 8981.

plainLanguage.summary: An IPv6 address is in two parts: the network prefix and an identifier for the interface itself. That second part normally comes from the hardware and never changes, so the same string appears in every connection a device makes. This RFC has the device generate a fresh random identifier at intervals and use it for outgoing connections, so that an observer cannot tie the connections together.

subtitle: Making an IPv6 address change over time so a device is harder to follow around the network.

tldr.problem: An IPv6 address is built from a network prefix and an interface identifier, and the interface identifier is normally taken from the interface's own hardware address. Because it never changes, anyone who can see traffic can link a person's activity in one place to their activity in another.
tldr.mechanism: A node keeps a randomized interface identifier that it regenerates periodically from an MD5 hash. Each new identifier is combined with the advertised prefixes to make temporary addresses, which are used for outgoing connections and are deprecated after a fixed time.
tldr.outcome: RFC 4941 is a Draft Standard from September 2007 and has been obsoleted by RFC 8981, which restates the same privacy extensions for IPv6 stateless address autoconfiguration.

facts.label: Hash used for the identifier
facts.value: MD5, though another algorithm may be used

today: RFC 4941 is a Draft Standard from September 2007, and it has been obsoleted by RFC 8981, which restates the privacy extensions for IPv6 stateless address autoconfiguration. The RFC itself notes that it obsoletes RFC 3041 and lists the nine changes an implementer of that earlier document should be aware of.

sections.title: The Problem With a Fixed Interface Identifier
sections.content:
Stateless address autoconfiguration lets an IPv6 node build its own addresses without a DHCP server. On an interface that carries an embedded IEEE identifier, the interface identifier is normally derived from that hardware address, and the result is likely to be globally unique. The interface identifier is then appended to a prefix to make a 128-bit address. Because the identifier stays constant, the same string appears in every address the node ever uses, which lets an observer link activity across different places and times.

The RFC names two ways the correlation can be done. An attacker on the path between the node and its peers can read the addresses in the packets as they pass. An attacker with access to the communication logs of the peers can find the same addresses in the records.

Because the identifier is embedded in the address, and the address is needed for communication at all, it cannot simply be hidden. IPv4 has a milder version of the same problem, but there the whole address usually changes when the address changes. IPv6 splits the address into a topology part and an interface part, so a device that moves to a different network keeps the same interface identifier inside a different address. A laptop used at home and at the office therefore leaves a trail that a server logging source addresses can follow, and any data-mining tool that correlates on addresses can be extended to correlate on the identifier instead.
sections.plainLanguage: The identifier that comes from the hardware never changes, and it appears in every address the device sends. Anyone watching the network or reading a server's logs can therefore recognise the device wherever it goes, even though the network part of the address has changed.

sections.title: Generating a Randomized Interface Identifier
sections.content:
The RFC generates a sequence of interface identifiers that looks random from the outside, using an MD5 hash. A node may use another hash algorithm instead.

With stable storage available, the algorithm keeps a 64-bit history value. On the very first boot the history value is a random number chosen to be hard to guess. Each round takes the history value, appends the interface identifier derived from the hardware, computes the MD5 digest, takes the leftmost 64 bits of that digest and clears the universal and local bit so the identifier is marked as locally significant. The result is compared against the reserved identifiers and against the addresses already on the device; if it is unacceptable the node restarts the process using the rightmost 64 bits of the digest as the new history value. Finally the rightmost 64 bits of the digest are saved as the history value for the next round.

The history value buys something even though generating identifiers at random would be simpler in theory. Two nodes that pick the same randomized identifier would otherwise each notice the clash through duplicate address detection and then generate the same identifier again, because they run the same flawed random number generator. Because the hardware identifier, which is usually globally unique, is mixed into the calculation, two nodes that collide will produce different identifiers on the next attempt.

Without stable storage there is no history value across a restart, so the initial value is generated at random instead. The RFC suggests using configuration data that differs from one machine to another, such as a user identity, a security key or a serial number, appending random data to it and hashing the result.
sections.plainLanguage: The new identifier is produced by hashing together a changing secret, the previous result, and the hardware address. The changing secret is remembered between rounds so that each new identifier differs from the last, and so that two devices that happen to collide will not collide again in the same way.

sections.title: Creating and Replacing Temporary Addresses
sections.content:
When a node processes a router advertisement carrying a prefix for autoconfiguration, it creates a public address as usual and should also create a temporary address from the same randomized interface identifier. Using one identifier for all the prefixes keeps the number of multicast groups the host must join small, because a host joins the solicited-node multicast address for each unicast address it supports and that address depends only on the low-order bits.

The temporary address takes its lifetimes from the prefix. Its valid lifetime is the lower of the public address's valid lifetime and TEMP_VALID_LIFETIME, and its preferred lifetime is the lower of the public address's preferred lifetime and TEMP_PREFERRED_LIFETIME minus the desynchronisation factor. A temporary address is only created if that preferred lifetime is longer than the regeneration advance, and one with a zero preferred lifetime must never be created. Every temporary address, not just the first from a given identifier, must go through duplicate address detection; if the address is already in use the node generates a new randomized identifier and tries again, up to TEMP_IDGEN_RETRIES times, and logs an error if none succeeds.

When a temporary address becomes deprecated a replacement is generated. Except for the brief moment of regeneration, at most one temporary address per prefix should be in a non-deprecated state at a time, and a new one should be started slightly before its predecessor is deprecated so that a preferred address is always available. When an interface connects to a new link, a new randomized identifier and a new set of temporary addresses should be generated immediately, so that addresses from the two links cannot easily be tied together.
sections.plainLanguage: Each advertised prefix gives the node a public address and, alongside it, a temporary address built from the current randomized identifier. The temporary one has its own clock: after a day it stops being preferred and after a week it stops being valid, and a replacement is created before the old one expires. Every new address is checked for duplicates before it is used.

sections.title: The Defined Constants
sections.content:
The RFC defines a small set of constants that control the timing, and it expects implementations to let users and administrators change them. TEMP_VALID_LIFETIME has a default of one week and is how long a temporary address stays valid. TEMP_PREFERRED_LIFETIME has a default of one day and is how long it stays preferred, and it is also the default interval at which a new randomized identifier is generated.

REGEN_ADVANCE is five seconds, the amount of time before a temporary address would be deprecated at which the replacement process starts. MAX_DESYNC_FACTOR is ten minutes and is the upper bound on DESYNC_FACTOR, which is a random value computed once at system start and never greater than TEMP_VALID_LIFETIME minus REGEN_ADVANCE. The desynchronisation factor exists so that many clients do not all change their addresses at the same moment. TEMP_IDGEN_RETRIES has a default of three and is how many times a node will try again after duplicate address detection reports a clash.
sections.plainLanguage: Four numbers set the pace: how long a temporary address stays preferred (a day), how long it stays valid (a week), how early the replacement is started (five seconds), and how many times a duplicate is retried (three). A random offset of up to ten minutes is added so that many devices do not all rotate at once.

sections.title: What Changing the Address Does Not Hide
sections.content:
The RFC is careful about the limits of the scheme. The network prefix is also a constant identifier, so every node at, say, one home shares it and can be grouped together. If a prefix is used by only one node, changing the interface identifier does not improve privacy at all, and the procedures are most effective when the prefix is not very static or is shared by a fair number of nodes.

A DNS name is another constant identifier. Changing the address does nothing about it unless the name changes as well, and the RFC notes that many nodes need a stable name because servers generally require one. Some servers refuse clients for which they cannot find a reverse DNS name, and may then check that the name maps back to the same address, so a client whose address is not registered may be unable to reach some services. The answer it suggests is that a node could register its temporary addresses under random names.

Two further limits are named. An attacker on the path may still correlate traffic by the contents of the packets and by their size and timing, and temporary addresses do not prevent that. And the RFC says plainly that the method is believed to be ineffective against sophisticated forms of traffic analysis.
sections.plainLanguage: Temporary addresses do not make a device invisible. The network part of the address stays the same, a DNS name usually stays the same, and an observer can still tell traffic apart by its size, its timing and its contents.

sections.title: Security Considerations and Deployment
sections.content:
The security section raises a conflict with a defensive measure. Ingress filtering is used to stop spoofed source addresses being used in denial of service attacks. Because a network with many nodes creates new temporary addresses at a fairly high rate, it may become hard for ingress filtering to tell a legitimately changing temporary address from a spoofed one that uses a topologically correct prefix with an interface identifier that does not exist. The RFC suggests using access control on a per-address basis at the network egress point instead.

The deployment section gives the other half. Devices must offer the user a way to turn temporary addresses on and off, and trusted administrators should be able to do the same, since a site may want them off to make debugging simpler. Per-prefix control should also be available, so that a site can leave temporary addresses off for unique local prefixes while enabling them for global ones, or enable them only for particular ranges, and that per-prefix setting should override the global one.

The RFC recommends that temporary addresses be disabled by default, because some servers refuse clients they cannot resolve and some applications misbehave when an address expires before they finish or when they expect several sessions to use the same address. Individual applications that know how long their connections last may override that. Finally, implementations must let the user or a trusted administrator override the use of temporary addresses altogether, since tracking down operational problems becomes harder when addresses keep changing.
sections.plainLanguage: Temporary addresses make it harder for a network to spot a forged source address, and they make troubleshooting harder. The RFC therefore says the feature should be off by default, that users and administrators should be able to switch it on or off, and that the choice can be made per prefix.

fields.name: Network prefix
fields.desc: The part of the address that describes where the node is attached to the network. It changes when the node moves.

fields.name: Interface identifier
fields.desc: The part that identifies the interface. Normally derived from the hardware address, and normally constant, which is the problem this RFC addresses.

items.label: 1 week
items.desc: How long a temporary address stays valid. Users should be able to override the default.

items.label: 1 day
items.desc: How long a temporary address stays preferred, and the default interval for generating a new randomized interface identifier.

items.label: 5 seconds
items.desc: How long before a temporary address would be deprecated the replacement process starts.

items.label: 10 minutes
items.desc: Upper bound on the desynchronisation factor.

items.label: Random, up to the maximum
